sections.heading: PQ Key Pre-Registration Design
sections.summary: Pre-registration allows stakers to claim a PQ key without depositing ETH; withdrawal credentials preferred over operator signing for authorization.
sections.body:
- Pre-registration (derived from EIP-8205) lets a staker make a free pre-agreement binding a PQ key to a validator before depositing ETH, removing the current requirement to put 1 ETH at risk in a race condition.
  - Pre-registrations expire and have limits, already handled by the EIP-8205 design.
- Proof of possession of the XMSS key is verified on the EL contract; the proof is not stored on-chain and no aggregation is needed.
  - Gas cost estimates for signature verification are approximately 20k–45k gas, considered manageable even for large staking pools.
  - Gas cost numbers for proof-of-possession verification linked: [pq-staking-contracts](https://github.com/ethereum/pq-staking-contracts/tree/main/contracts#gas-of-the-proof-of-possession)
- Discussion of whether the operator (BLS key holder) or withdrawal credentials should authorize the PQ key rotation:
  - Lido/Dima argued strongly against using the validator private key: operators may have generated keys inside TEEs with no ability to extract them, and historically all credential rotations (0x00→0x01, 0x01→0x02) have used withdrawal credentials.
  - Potuz initially favored withdrawal credentials and noted that allowing operator signing would force client teams to implement new signing paths.
  - Pawan and Barnabas agreed that the validator private key should not be used for non-duty operations.
  - Cayman noted the mental model that the operator holds a lower-credentialed token granted by withdrawal credentials, making it counterintuitive for the lower-credentialed party to create the new PQ token.
- Agreement: keep it simple, stick to withdrawal credentials for authorization. No decision to support both paths.

sections.heading: EIP and Spec Status
sections.summary: The EIP is outdated and will be updated by end of week; the PQ consensus spec is built on top of Glamsterdam.
sections.body:
- The existing EIP for PQ is outdated relative to the consensus spec.
  - Plan: update the EIP by end of week, keep it brief and open-ended enough to allow spec-level changes, and merge it to get an EIP number.
- Two spec artifacts exist: a PR for pre-registration built on Heze, and a PQ Gasper branch built on Glamsterdam.
  - Working on top of Glamsterdam was decided at Devcon as an emergency-preparedness measure.
  - Justin will rebase as needed; Glamsterdam is the easier base for current processing.
- Goal for this week's breakout sessions: produce a spec that client teams can start coding against.

sections.heading: Proof of Possession on EL
sections.summary: Proof of possession of the XMSS key will be verified entirely on the EL; the CL receives only the pub key and withdrawal credential.
sections.body:
- The XMSS proof of possession is provided as calldata to the pre-registration contract on the EL; the contract verifies it and drops the signature.
  - No signature data is stored on-chain; the CL receives only the pub key.
- If BLS verification were also added on the EL, operator-initiated registration would become possible (two signature verifications), but the group preferred not to add that complexity.
- Terence confirmed: the proof of possession does not even need to be passed to the CL.

sections.heading: Fork Transition: Exiting BLS Validators and Slashing
sections.summary: Unregistered BLS validators will be exited immediately at the PQ fork with a long withdrawability delay; cross-fork slashing will rely on social consensus.
sections.body:
- At the PQ fork, validators without registered PQ keys will have their exits initiated immediately (not queued through the regular churn).
  - Their withdrawability epoch will be set far in the future (e.g., ~8,000 epochs / roughly a month) so their stake remains locked and theoretically slashable.
- No on-chain processing of BLS slashings after the fork:
  - Analyzing every cross-fork slashing condition (e.g., surround votes with one leg pre-fork and one post-fork) is extremely complex.
  - Agreement: rely on social consensus — accountability is preserved because equivocation proofs can be constructed off-chain, and a trivial hard fork could burn the offending stake if needed.
  - Social slashing has never been done before and would require a hard fork plus community coordination, but the scenario is considered a theoretical edge case.
- Francesco D'Amato suggested exiting all BLS validators at once but keeping the withdrawal period to a few weeks; this was well received.
- No separate exit queue will be introduced; the same queue is used but with a delayed withdrawability epoch.
- Potuz emphasized that the fork itself is simple on the CL side; the hard part is social coordination around the transition.

sections.heading: PQ Fork Activation Threshold
sections.summary: No 2/3 registration threshold needed; the fork will be scheduled when a minimum stake is registered, similar to beacon chain genesis.
sections.body:
- The spec originally suggested requiring 2/3 of validators to have registered PQ keys before activating the fork.
- Multiple participants (Barnabas, ethDreamer, Potuz) argued this coupling is unnecessary and could let laggards delay the transition.
  - Barnabas: the fork should happen when developers are ready; unregistered validators simply lose duties.
  - ethDreamer: at beacon chain launch, only a minimum stake threshold was required, not a fraction of all capital.
- Agreement: use a minimum stake threshold (similar to beacon chain genesis), not a fraction of the validator set. If the threshold is met before the scheduled time, wait for activation; if not met, delay.
- No ENR signaling or new gossip topic for PQ readiness will be added; it is assumed that validators who register PQ keys will be ready for the fork, same as any other hard fork.

sections.heading: Voluntary Exits as Execution Requests
sections.summary: CL-gossiped voluntary exits will be replaced by EL execution requests to avoid large PQ signatures on the CL P2P layer.
sections.body:
- The PQ spec removes CL-gossiped voluntary exits and replaces them with a new voluntary exit execution request on the EL.
  - Motivation: PQ signatures are much larger than BLS, making CL P2P DoS protection harder; execution requests already have an EL fee market for DoS mitigation.
  - The CL would otherwise need to download and validate large XMSS signatures over gossip for voluntary exits.
- Potuz: the EL approach is safer; execution requests work well for this. Even removing voluntary exits entirely would be better than keeping the CL gossip path with large PQ signatures.
- A known issue (from Lido): someone can spam small withdrawal requests to keep the pending-balance-to-withdraw nonzero, blocking operator-initiated exits. This is an existing problem, not PQ-specific, and will not be addressed in the PQ fork.
- Agreement: proceed with execution requests for voluntary exits; keep scope minimal.

sections.heading: Committee and Subnet Reduction
sections.summary: Committees and subnets will both be reduced to 16; the original spec mistakenly only reduced subnets.
sections.body:
- The original PQ spec reduced subnets from 64 to 16 but left committees at 64, which was identified as a mistake — the number of proofs scales with committees, not subnets.
  - With 64 committees and 16 subnets, each subnet would have 4 committees producing 4+ aggregates, requiring an extra aggregation layer.
- Agreement: reduce both committees and subnets to 16, making each committee ~4× larger.
  - This eliminates the need for an intermediate aggregation layer within subnets.
  - Trade-off: larger committees mean each aggregation takes longer (~2–2.5 seconds), but this fits within slot timing.
- No objections were raised to the 16/16 configuration.

sections.heading: Aggregator Selection: RANDAO vs VRF
sections.summary: Aggregators will be selected via RANDAO (not VRF) with a 2-epoch lookahead stored in the beacon state; balance weighting is desirable but secondary.
sections.body:
- Current VRF-based aggregator selection can result in committees with zero aggregators when the expected count is low (e.g., 4). RANDAO-based selection guarantees exactly the target number.
- Potuz's key constraint: gossip message validation must not require recreating a beacon state; aggregator assignments must be derivable from cached or head state data.
  - PTC-style selection (computed at epoch transition, stored in beacon state) satisfies this — any state from the same branch has the correct assignments.
  - Storing aggregator indices in the beacon state was put at ~32 KiB for 16 aggregators per committee, or 4× that if more — a number its author explicitly did not vouch for, and negligible either way against the ~300+ MB beacon state.
- Balance-weighted selection discussed at length:
  - Francesco D'Amato: uniform selection over-represents small validators (a 32 ETH validator is 64× more likely to be selected than a max validator per unit of stake); balance-weighted is the fair default.
  - Potuz was skeptical that balance weighting would change outcomes in practice given most large operators still run 32 ETH validators and haven't consolidated.
  - Consensus leaned toward balance-weighted as more principled, but it was acknowledged as secondary to the RANDAO/lookahead design.
- Terence summarized the working parameters: 16 subnets, 16 committees, 4 aggregators per subnet, stored in beacon state, balance-weighted selection.
- Mikhail asked whether reducing aggregators was even necessary if committees were reduced to 16 — keeping 16 aggregators per committee with the existing VRF would avoid complexity. This was noted but not resolved.

sections.heading: Aggregation Bandwidth and Slot Timing
sections.summary: 64 aggregate proofs (~6.25 MiB) on the global topic is too much bandwidth; reducing to 16 is still large; this is the main unresolved blocker.
sections.body:
- With 4 aggregators × 16 committees = 64 proofs (~100 KiB each) flowing through the global topic, total bandwidth is ~6.25 MiB per slot — identified as prohibitively high.
  - Even 16 aggregate proofs (one per committee) is considered a lot.
  - Mikhail: 6.25 MiB/s is huge; even 16 aggregates would be too much.
- Strategies discussed:
  - Having aggregators do a 4→1 merge within each committee before posting to the global topic, but this adds another recursion layer.
  - Staggering aggregator broadcast times so the last aggregator can incorporate earlier ones.
  - The IGNORE rule (drop aggregates that are subsets of already-seen ones) helps but is brittle and not worst-case robust.
- Proposer-side recursion timing:
  - 16→1 recursion benchmarked at ~1.3s on AVX2 (EX63, 8 threads) in isolation; estimated 2–3 seconds under real-world conditions with other node workloads.
  - 4→1 should be faster than 16→1 and was confirmed as roughly linear, but no number has been benchmarked yet; adding the layer further compresses available time.
- Attestation broadcast at 3s into the slot leaves ~5 seconds for aggregation + global propagation + proposer recursion — very tight.
- Potuz noted the proposer must also aggregate attestations from previous slots (not just current), making the actual recursion larger than the committee count.
  - Silver lining: proposers and aggregators can begin pre-aggregating earlier in the slot.
- Multiple participants (Francesco, Potuz, Luca, Barnabas) suggested that if slot timing cannot accommodate PQ aggregation, a minimal version of decoupled consensus (DC) should be pursued instead of extending slot times.
- Builder fallback discussed: Potuz proposed that builders (via direct connections) could provide aggregates as a sidecar alongside bids. Titan expressed interest.
  - Strong pushback from soispoke, Pawan, Justin: relying on builders is brittle and incentivizes client forking.
  - Agreement: builder aggregation could be an optional fallback but must not be the primary path.
- Topic flagged as the main unresolved blocker; to be continued in the next session.

sections.heading: Client Implementation Status and Devnet Planning
sections.summary: Lodestar and ethlambda have tested LeanVM bindings; Prysm has not started; goal is a codeable spec this week to begin prototyping.
sections.body:
- Lodestar: has tested LeanVM bindings and has disposable code for the half-spec.
- ethlambda: has tested LeanVM bindings and implemented EIP-8483 on top of Heze; will rebase onto Glamsterdam and continue with the rest of the spec.
- Prysm/Potuz: has not started on LeanVM bindings; plans to hand-roll assembly for XMSS signing paths; the STARK part will initially be a black box.
- Lighthouse (ethDreamer): pointed to [lean-pq-bindings](https://github.com/ethereum/lean-pq-bindings) for the wrapper; since Lighthouse uses Rust, may not need the bindings layer.
- LeanVM benchmarks available at [leanvm.org](https://leanvm.org/).
  - soispoke suggested a "soft LeanVM freeze" declaring a worst-case baseline so benchmarks stop being a moving target.
  - Tom Wambsgans committed to running benchmarks with EL workloads running side-by-side.
  - Barnabas requested benchmarks that include block building (not just verification) alongside mainnet-like EL execution with 200M+ gas.
- Potuz committed to having benchmarks on his current validating node (64 GB memory) by the next day.
- Francesco D'Amato stressed that the main open question is aggregation feasibility, not the spec per se, and called for a large globally distributed devnet.
  - Mikhail asked whether a devnet focused only on aggregation (without the full advanced spec) would be possible.
- Overall plan: finalize a codeable spec this week, then prototype across clients to test whether PQ + Gasper aggregation is viable within slot timing constraints.
